3030 Deathwar Redux – A Space Odyssey is an indie space adventure developed by Bird in Sky and published by Crunchy Leaf Games. The game originally began as a smaller project before being reworked into the expanded Redux edition released on Steam in 2017, bringing improved visuals, additional content, and refined mechanics. At its core, the game blends multiple genres into a single experience: open-world space exploration, trading simulation, arcade-style combat, and narrative-driven adventure elements. While it may not have the technical scale of major space simulators, it manages to carve out its own identity through a mix of humor, retro aesthetics, and surprising gameplay depth.

The story unfolds in the year 3030 in a galaxy still recovering from a catastrophic technological disaster. Long ago, mysterious self-replicating machines known as the Cleaners devastated many inhabited worlds, leaving large portions of space dangerous or uninhabitable. Humanity and several alien civilizations survived the catastrophe by retreating into space stations and isolated colonies scattered across the galaxy. Players step into the role of John Falcon, an underpaid and somewhat unlucky space pilot who finds himself pulled into a web of conspiracy and intrigue after a routine delivery job goes wrong. What begins as a simple attempt to make a living gradually evolves into a much larger story involving secret factions, hidden technology, and unanswered questions about the origins of the Cleaners.

The game presents its universe through a semi-open sandbox structure that allows players to travel freely between star systems. Each system contains space stations, asteroid belts, derelict ships, and other points of interest. Navigation takes place in a top-down perspective as players guide Falcon’s ship through space while monitoring radar, fuel, and potential threats. The design evokes classic space trading games from earlier decades, where players slowly build their reputation and resources by completing missions, transporting goods, and exploring new sectors of the galaxy.

Combat plays a significant role in the experience, particularly when dealing with pirates or hostile factions. Battles occur in real time as players maneuver their ship while firing lasers, missiles, or other weapons. Because many enemies are faster or better equipped, positioning and quick reactions become important for survival. Upgrading weapons and defensive systems becomes essential as the story progresses and enemies grow more dangerous. These encounters add excitement to the otherwise exploratory nature of the game and provide opportunities for players to test their ship configurations.

Economic progression is another major component of gameplay. Players can earn credits by accepting delivery jobs, transporting passengers, mining resources, salvaging abandoned ships, or hunting down criminals for bounties. The galaxy operates as a living marketplace where goods can be bought in one location and sold at another for profit. Managing cargo space, fuel costs, and risk levels becomes part of the strategic decision making. Successful traders can accumulate enough wealth to purchase larger ships with greater cargo capacity or better combat capabilities.

One of the more interesting gameplay variations appears when players dock at stations or board derelict spacecraft. At these moments the perspective changes, shifting from the top-down space view into side-scrolling exploration segments. Players can walk through station interiors, talk to characters, search rooms for clues, and accept story missions. These sections introduce light adventure game elements, including dialogue trees and investigative tasks that help advance the narrative. The writing during these sequences often includes humorous exchanges and quirky characters, giving the game a playful personality.

Derelict ship exploration is particularly memorable because it introduces a different style of gameplay. When players encounter abandoned vessels drifting through space, they can board them to search for valuable salvage. Inside these ships, the game becomes a side-scrolling exploration challenge where players navigate damaged corridors, fight strange alien creatures, and collect resources. These missions provide a welcome change of pace from standard space travel and reinforce the sense that the galaxy is full of hidden dangers and forgotten relics.

Ship customization is another important feature that allows players to tailor their experience. Over time, Falcon can purchase new ships that specialize in different roles such as cargo hauling, combat, or exploration. Each vessel can be upgraded with various modules including stronger shields, faster engines, advanced scanners, and improved weapon systems. Deciding how to configure a ship becomes an important strategic element depending on whether the player prefers trading, combat, or exploration as their primary activity.

Visually, 3030 Deathwar Redux embraces a retro-inspired art style that reflects its roots in classic space games. The galaxy map is filled with colorful nebulae, bright star systems, and detailed ship sprites that give the universe a distinctive look. Character portraits and station interiors resemble old-school adventure games, with pixel-inspired artwork that adds to the nostalgic charm. While the graphics may appear simple compared to modern space simulations, the cohesive style helps create a memorable and consistent visual identity.

The audio design complements the game’s atmosphere with electronic music that captures the feeling of drifting through deep space. Ambient tracks play during exploration, creating a calm and sometimes lonely mood while traveling between distant systems. During combat or tense moments, the soundtrack becomes more energetic, adding excitement to encounters with hostile ships. Sound effects for weapons, engines, and environmental interactions help bring the universe to life without overwhelming the player.

Despite its creativity, the game does have some limitations. One of the most noticeable is the amount of time spent traveling between star systems, which can slow the pace of the experience during certain missions. While this design choice reinforces the sense of scale in the galaxy, it can sometimes lead to repetitive travel segments. Additionally, some mission types—particularly cargo deliveries—can feel similar after repeated play sessions.

The interface and control scheme may also take some time to master, especially for players unfamiliar with space simulation mechanics. Managing navigation systems, cargo inventories, and ship upgrades involves several menus and controls that can initially feel overwhelming. However, once players become comfortable with the systems, the gameplay begins to flow more naturally.

Ultimately, 3030 Deathwar Redux – A Space Odyssey is an ambitious indie title that successfully combines several gameplay styles into a cohesive adventure. Its mix of space trading, combat, exploration, and narrative storytelling creates a rich sandbox where players can shape their own journey through the galaxy. While the game occasionally struggles with pacing and interface complexity, its charm, humor, and creative design make it a memorable experience.

For players who enjoy retro-inspired space adventures with open exploration and a sense of discovery, 3030 Deathwar Redux offers a surprisingly deep journey through a colorful and unpredictable universe. It may not match the scale of larger space simulators, but its creativity and personality ensure that it remains a standout entry in the indie space exploration genre.

[h1]A unique game with a funny name, this one speaks to a lot of segments of gamers and features delightful pixel art and an outstanding soundtrack. If you were a fan of old-school Privateer, give this one a look.[/h1]

In gaming, space is interesting. It's limitless and yet somehow jam-packed with games set there. You name the genre, there are thousands of space games in it already. It's a crowded field and a lot of it is mediocre at best. But occasionally, a really good game peeks through. A game that checks off a lot of boxes without feeling forced. This is such a game. Enormous universe to explore? Check. A variety of ships you can buy and pilot? Check. Lots of upgrades for those ships? Check. Good graphics, great soundtrack? Check and check. Lots of aphids to smash? Oddly enough, check.

[h2]What do you feel like doing?[/h2]
Go for it. 
[h3]"Open world" done right [/h3]
This is one of those games that says "open world" and [i]means[/i] it. Much like the grandfather of the genre, Wing Commander Privateer, 3030 Deathwar Redux lets you forge your way as you see fit. Mine asteroids, ship trade goods, run transport contracts, salvage derelicts, hunt pirates, [i]be[/i] a pirate - it's all up to you. Make your fortune the way you choose. If you're the self-determining type, mining is a good path to riches. 

[h3]Salvage for fun and profit [/h3]
Salvaging derelicts isn't a gimmick; it's fun and profitable. The game shifts you out of top-down spaceflight mode so you can navigate through the wreck in a spacesuit, picking up worthwhile salvage, recovering bodies, and if you're particularly lucky, saving survivors - all of which is worth substantial money. 

[h3]Delightfully simplistic combat [/h3]
Combat is somewhat simplistic but it's fun. With only two dimensions to work with, it's straightforward and doesn't require spatial orientation skills. Get your enemy in sight and pour fire on them until they explode. Some targets are easier than others, and wanted pirates are going to give you a tough fight (as will security forces if you decide to go the pirate route) but with adequate tools and talent, you can win out.

[h3]Large menu of ships and upgrades [/h3]
Where a lot of games fall down is that you can make a lot more money than there are things to do with it. 3030 Deathwar Redux largely sidesteps this problem: you have a large list of ships you can choose to buy and upgrade. It's not perfect - more on that later - but there's a lot of leg to the shop. 

[h3]Such a fantastic soundtrack [/h3]
And the soundtrack. Oh, the soundtrack. If you've never heard of The Kyoto Connection, don't worry, this game will fix that. The soundtrack meshes perfectly with the tone and tenor of the game and is one of the few I don't turn off. Along with that, the game's audio design is also spot on for what it should be.

[h3]Oh, and aphids [/h3]
Oh, and the aphids remark above? Not a joke. Space stations aren't known for cleanliness, and there are aphids on the computer consoles from time to time. Just do everyone a favor and smash them. (Don't worry if bugs aren't okay with you; there's a menu option to disable them.)

[h2]What don't you feel like doing?[/h2]
Okay, so 3030 Deathwar Redux isn't a perfect game. Very few are. Fortunately, the problems with this game are few and, for the most part, not really problems.
[h3]Little direction, find your own path [/h3]
The biggest issue is that this game gives you very little direction. If you're the self-starting, self-guiding type, that's fine. But if you need a clear overarching story in your games, well, you're going to feel lost in this one. Is there a main quest story to follow? ...maybe? It's not really obvious if there is, but there's so much to see and do that if you're the explore-and-interact type, it won't bother you.
[h3]Learn by trying [/h3]
The game also doesn't explain some core concepts very clearly. The design intent appears to be a "try things out and see what happens" philosophy, but that could feel a little uncomfortable if you're risk-averse. (Fortunately, as long as you're not running a mission you can save whenever you're docked, so save before trying something new in case things go sideways on you.)
[h3]Slow pace of upgrade unlocks [/h3]
There's a substantial list of ships and upgrades, but upgrades unlock [i]slowly.[/i] So you will often accumulate cash faster than you will unlock things to spend it on. In a way that's nice because you don't feel like you're falling behind, but at the same time it doesn't give you much to reach for other than the belief that there's more to buy coming eventually.

[h1]The Bottom Line[/h1]
This is a [i]fun[/i] game. If you liked Privateer, you'll probably like this. If you like semi-lightweight space games that give you a lot of freedom and good music to enjoy while doing it, you'll probably love this. Is it $15 good? Actually... yes, it is. If you can get it on sale, great, but it's worth full price.

3030 Deathwar Redux - A Space Odyssey is a jack of all trades title but master of none, except atmosphere. The atmosphere is absolutely phenomenal. For example, as you look through the trade screen within a station, little bugs usually cross the screen, which you can crush with your mouse pointer. Sometimes a lizard crosses the screen too, as if it's going after its next meal. This has almost no effect on gameplay but are just there to set the scene. Before docking at a station, you need to hail them and, if you want, you can ask further questions. Why? For immersion. While inside the station, there are full of little things going on that immediately catches your eye. When you visit one of the bars in a station then you can banter with many others for no other reason than world building and for fun. Hell, you can even eventually buy a bio-scanner and then scan everyone at a station just to see their details. You can hail other ships, explore wrecks with all its debris inside (specifically to gather map charts for the nebula), shoot debris in space, tractor in items, upgrading specific parts of your ship, take advantage of the game's economy (e.g. sell high and buy low), taxi others, and many more. Items found when exploring ship wrecks will usually have their own eye catching little story or description (e.g. tons of unique and bizarre magazines). Whenever you enter or leave a wreck or station, a little animation plays, sometimes specifically for the ship your flying. There are so many jobs one can take, buy ships specifically for what you want to do (e.g. fight, trade or a mix) and there are even numerous reputation systems.  And I must say, the soundtrack is absolutely fantastic, which really sets the scene. I'll sometimes just fly through space a little more just to jam to the song currently playing.

Unfortunately, the controls and UI are clunky, which can make exploring or doing a mission really frustrating. Sadly, after touching on many of the gameplay aspects, it would be nice to have a really indepth system to really sink my teeth into, but this title lacks this. However, as a 2d Han Solo-esque space adventure with a bit of Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy comedy it really has so much charm. One can attempt to get more involved within this universe but I think the story and atmosphere are where its strength lies. And, it's not every game where you can fly in space, salvage a wreck, hunt some pirates (or others) and then dock in a station (or pirate space station) to sell your loot or pay someone to change the licence plate and then banter with the NPCs. It would be great if this type of interaction existed in games like Starsector.  I would love a sequel or more games like this.

I highly recommend this title to any and all interested in this genre.

Un'avventura open-world che preme sull'acceleratore della nostalgia e propone un mix eterogeneo di elementi che danno vita ad un insieme dannatamente accattivante. Questa odissea spaziale segue le gesta di John Falcon, pilota mercenario e cacciatore di taglie, con il look alla Indiana Jones. Ricorda qualcuno? Il citazionismo non si limita al personaggio principale ma si estende ad una trama declinata perlopiù in maniera umoristica. Non mancano comunque momenti più dark ed un paio di buoni colpi di scena. 
Il gameplay di 3030 Deathwar Redux è suddiviso principalmente in tre sezioni. Passeremo la maggior parte del tempo a pilotare l'astronave di Falcon con una visuale dall'alto. Nello spazio la lista di missioni che non seguono la trama principale e che ci permettono di guadagnare preziosi crediti ha una discreta varietà, sebbene non eccelsa. Si comincia con semplici lavori da tassista o corriere spaziale, ma una volta che riusciremo ad acquistare una nave dotata di armi verranno sbloccate missioni di scorta o che prevedono di dare la caccia ad una flottiglia di pirati. Ed è qui che la colonna sonora riveste la parte del leone. Il pop elettronico e un po' ruffiano del gruppo The Kyoto Connection dà ottime vibrazioni e rende la navigazione nello spazio ancora più godibile. Quando ci troveremo all'interno di una stazione spaziale prenderemo il controllo del prode Falcon in una visuale a scorrimento laterale. Qui l'estetica da avventura grafica vecchio stile è al servizio della narrazione e della customizzazione della nostra nave. Saltuariamente nelle fasi più avanzate ci sarà anche qualche sparatoria. L'ultimo segmento riguarda l'esplorazione dei derelitti delle astronavi che all'inizio aggiunge ulteriore varietà ma finisce per stancare abbastanza in fretta. Questo non vale per il gioco nel suo insieme ed ho perso il conto di quante volte ho detto la fatidica frase "ancora un'altra missione e poi chiudo".

The Review:  

They took 10 years to make this game....TEN YEARS!  And it shows because the game is flawless!  

Its simplicity is what makes it work - it's just fun!  Pixel graphics!?  I mean, wtf!?  And yet....magic.  You just keep wanting to get out there and splash pirate scum all over the spacelanes!  Why?  To get the cash to install the stash to make the splash!  Bigger better guns, faster more explodery mis-kiles, and that marvellous looking superduperuber-ship!  

When you start the game you're earning hundreds - when you find a system that sells the top ships they're in the Millions!  You think you're never going to get there, but you earn some dough, you buy a bigger gun, you learn to kill bigger baddies, you haul more parcels, you buy another ship with passenger space, you turn into a taxi/delivery service.  Money comes in, you buy another ship that can actually turn^^  You shoot stuff, you try your first missile, you start to buy all the bits n bobs available to upgrade your ship.  You think, "Wow, this reward is 10k for this pirate....can I?"  You give it a go, you waste that mother....the world opens up to you.  One moment you're a newt, next you're a naughty-bottomed chocolate coconut bar capturer!  

It's just a joy to play, pure and simple.  The most common thing said about this game is the desire for it to be longer.  No greater compliment can be given to a game other than people want to Keep playing it.  But then the these things are considered marvels of their ilk exactly because they end before they unravel - how many things have we had/eaten/watched etc that we thought were absolutely brilliant....until they made another one, and then another.  The gem became cloudy, the heart of it slowly poisoned, the colour drained and the soul died.  Keep 'em wanting more.  

Oh, and the scanner thing - one mission!  You can scan EVERYONE!  The entire galaxy worth of characters, and it is pointless!  Just that one person for that one mission.  Shame they never expanded upon its use.  And the ship scanner too - let's face it, you're just gonna blow ship up regardless of its content^^  

Don't bother trying to map the clouds, it doesn't affect you enough to matter.  And for those on larger aspect ratios, the bottom of the screen has a tiny line of script that is vital in a later mission searching for a satellite - there's a verbal diarrhoea post in discussions from me exactly about it^^  

Just play it, it has a magic about it that makes it....magic.

Fun little Space Game!

To summarize, this is a great little game. Worth every penny, especially when it is on sale. The great soundtrack and the novel 2D point and click style are really good. I hope there will be a sequel, or another deeper game based on the same ideas.

I took it as a more relaxing game rather than a hardcore simulation and I had a lot of fun.

Just don’t take too much time to grind stuff. Enjoy the story! Or else you will be bored by the possible repetitiveness of the side quests. I played for about 18 hours without grinding, just having fun, and I was able to finish the story without problems.

What I liked:
* The soundtrack is incredibly great for such “little” game.
* The 2D graphics are charming.
* I love the 2D point and click interface when in station: This is much better than a menu or a crappy 3D rendering like in X4. It is quick and immersive. Plus, there are really pseudo point and click parts in the story!
* Freedom is here. Despite simple missions, you can decide how to grow your “character” and how go thought the story.

What could be better:
* The gameplay is good but repetitive. Maybe something like 10 different tasks. But that’s fine if you don’t grind: Just follow the story line, while doing side missions on the way…
* There is no real customization concerning your ship. There is a good variety of ships available of all kinds and tiers. However, equipment-wise, while you have a lot of modules to install, there is no real choice: just pick the most expensive one you can afford in each category. There is no “build” per say, like in Eve Online for example.

3030 Deathwar, what can you say about this game?  Killer music while cruising the stars, cargo trading, mining, and a bit of space combat to brighten your day.  If that's all it had, it would be an OK game, but it has a story that's actually pretty good in a cheesy sci-fi sort of way.  

So, if you like space sims, if you like flying around completing missions, and you want a fun plot to follow, this is for you.

It's easy to turn these kinds of games into a slog, where your missions around different star systems become rote and tedious, but somehow 3030 Deathwar avoids this.  I've been sticking to story missions in my last few hours, and still dip into doing side missions just because they're fun.  They're easy to get, easy to find, and solved quickly.  This makes for a really compelling game - the main missions are new things to do, but the side jobs are still fun, earn money for new toys, and encourage trying new things.  Really fun game, definitely worth full price if you like the genre.
